ourMissionText: Our mission is to democratize access to high-quality coding education, empowering all K-12 students, particularly Black and Brown children, to develop critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills. We equip students with the real programming skills, and experiences necessary to thrive in a technology-driven world, fostering a love of learning and preparing them for successful futures in diverse fields. We prioritize career readiness, especially for our high school students, providing pathways to in-demand tech careers through hands-on projects, mentorship, and industry connections. We strive to increase diversity within the tech sector by connecting students to internships, apprenticeships, and job opportunities, while cultivating an inclusive and supportive learning environment for all.
ourVisionText: To create a future where every student, regardless of background, has the skills, confidence, and opportunities to thrive in the digital age. We envision a world where coding is as fundamental as literacy, where Black and Brown students are equally represented in high-paying tech careers, and where diversity drives innovation in every industry. Through engaging, accessible education and strategic partnerships, we aim to empower the next generation to lead, create, and shape a more inclusive and equitable future in technology.

parentFaqQ1: How do I create an account for my child?
parentFaqA1: Creating an account is simple! Visit our sign-up page and select 'Parent Account'. Enter your email, create a password, and then add your child's profile. You can add multiple children under one parent account. Each child will have their own personalized learning dashboard.
parentFaqQ2: How can I monitor my child's progress?
parentFaqA2: Log into your parent dashboard to view real-time progress reports. You'll see completed lessons, earned badges, time spent learning, and skill assessments. We also send weekly progress summaries to your email highlighting key achievements and areas for improvement.
parentFaqQ3: How do I reset my child's password?
parentFaqA3: From your parent dashboard, select your child's profile and click 'Account Settings'. Choose 'Reset Password' and enter a new password. For additional security, we recommend using passwords that are easy for children to remember but hard to guess.
parentFaqQ4: How do I encourage my child to practice coding regularly?
parentFaqA4: Consistency is key! Set a regular practice schedule, celebrate achievements with them, and show interest in their projects. Our gamification features including badges, streaks, and leaderboards help motivate young learners. Consider coding together as a family activity!
parentFaqQ5: How do I contact support if I need help?
parentFaqA5: We're here to help! You can reach our support team via live chat (available 9 AM - 6 PM EST), email at support@codealgoacademy.com, or through our Help Center with searchable articles.
teacherFaqQ1: How do I set up a classroom for my students?
teacherFaqA1: Teachers can create a classroom by going to the Teacher Dashboard and clicking 'Create Classroom'. Enter your class name, grade level and click on submit.
teacherFaqQ2: How do I add Students to my classroom?
teacherFaqA2: Go to the Teacher Dashboard and click 'Student'. Then select 'Add Students' and enter student details.
teacherFaqA3: Use the Live class tab to view performance, completed levels, and engagement levels.
teacherFaqQ4: How will my student access the game?
teacherFaqA4: With the credentials you have provided. Your student can then log in to their account and choose to customize their character.
teacherFaqQ5: How do I access curriculum resources?
teacherFaqA5: Navigate to the Resources tab in your teacher dashboard. You'll find lesson plans, worksheets, presentation slides, and assessment rubrics organized by grade level and topic. All materials are aligned with CS education standards.
teacherFaqQ6: How do I generate progress reports for parents?
teacherFaqA6: Go to Reports > Student Progress in your dashboard. Select individual students or entire classes, choose the date range, and click Generate Report. Reports can be exported as PDF or shared directly via email to parents.
teacherFaqQ7: How do I manage student accounts?
teacherFaqA7: In your Classroom Settings, you can add, remove, or edit student profiles. Reset passwords, transfer students between classes, and set individual learning paths. Bulk import is available via CSV for larger classes.

about.heading: How CodeAlgo Academy works
about.intro: CodeAlgo Academy is a learning platform where children pick up real coding skills by playing. It is used by families at home and by teachers in classrooms, and it is built around a few simple ideas.

topics.title: Learning through play
topics.body: Lessons take place inside a 3D game. Students solve challenges by writing instructions for their character, and the game responds straight away, so they can see what worked and fix what did not. Children stay motivated because they want to reach the next level, and they practice real coding concepts while they do it.

topics.title: From blocks to Python
topics.body: New coders begin with block coding, where they snap instructions together and learn how sequences, loops, and conditions work. When they are ready, they move on to Python and start typing real code. The thinking stays the same from one stage to the next, so each step builds on the last.

topics.title: Coding, math, and AI literacy together
topics.body: Coding is a practical way to use math. Students count, measure, spot patterns, and reason step by step as they play, and they are introduced to how artificial intelligence works and how to use it responsibly. The goal is confident problem solvers, not only children who can follow instructions.

topics.title: Built for families
topics.body: Parents create an account, add a profile for each child, and follow their progress from a parent dashboard. They can see what their child has completed and how much time they have spent, and they can set screen time limits that suit their household.

topics.title: Built for classrooms
topics.body: Teachers set up classes and add students with Clever, Google Classroom, or manual entry. Younger students can sign in with printed QR code cards. Progress reports show who needs support and who is ready for more, and CodeAlgo runs in the browser on the Chromebooks and computers schools already have.

topics.title: Who we work with
topics.body: CodeAlgo Academy is used by parents teaching at home, by classroom teachers, and by schools, districts, charter networks, and after-school programs. Whatever the setting, the aim is the same: give every child a fair chance to learn how technology is made, and the confidence to make it themselves. If you would like to bring CodeAlgo to your family or your school, our team is glad to help you get started.

topics.title: A path to real opportunity
topics.body: Our work does not stop at the last level. Students learn to think through problems, write real programs, and then put those skills to use through internships with companies. We are based in Kansas City, Missouri, and we are committed to opening careers in technology to students who have too often been left out of them.

parents.heading: A parent's guide to coding at home
parents.intro: You do not need to know how to code to help your child learn. What matters most is a steady routine, a safe setup, and a parent who shows interest. These habits make the biggest difference.

topics.title: Getting started
topics.body: Create your parent account first, then add a profile for each child. Sit with your child for the first session so you can see how the game works and what a lesson looks like. Let them hold the mouse or tablet while you ask questions. Ten or fifteen minutes is enough for a first try, and stopping while it is still fun makes them want to come back.

topics.title: Online safety
topics.body: Keep the device in a shared room, such as the kitchen or living room, especially for younger children. Use a password your child can remember but others cannot guess, and remind them never to share it. Check friend requests together and talk about why we only connect with people we know. Make it normal for your child to tell you when something online feels wrong.

topics.title: Managing screen time
topics.body: Short, regular sessions work better than one long one. Twenty to thirty minutes, three or four times a week, is a good rhythm for most children. Agree on the schedule in advance so there is less arguing when it is time to stop. You can set screen time limits from your parent account, and it helps to balance coding with outdoor play, reading, and sleep.

topics.title: Tracking progress
topics.body: Open your parent dashboard once a week and look at what your child completed, how long they spent, and which skills they are building. Look for patterns over time: a week with little progress usually means a level is too hard or interest is dropping. Use what you see to start a conversation, not to check up on them.

topics.title: Encouraging learning
topics.body: Praise effort and persistence more than speed. When your child gets stuck, ask what they have tried and what they could change, instead of giving the answer. Getting code wrong and fixing it is how every programmer learns, so treat mistakes as a normal part of the work. Celebrate badges and finished levels, and ask your child to teach you what they learned.

topics.title: When your child gets frustrated
topics.body: Every learner hits a level that feels impossible. When that happens, suggest a short break, then come back and read the problem together out loud. Ask your child to explain what the code should do, step by step, because saying it aloud often reveals the mistake. If they are still stuck, it is fine to leave the level for another day. Remind them of an earlier challenge that once felt hard and now feels easy. Learning to keep going through frustration is one of the most useful things coding teaches.

topics.title: Family coding activities
topics.body: Coding ideas fit into everyday life. Ask your child to write exact step-by-step instructions for making a sandwich, then follow them literally and laugh at what goes wrong. Draw a maze on paper and guide each other through it using only forward, left, and right. Take turns on a level, or let an older sibling coach a younger one. These games build the same thinking the lessons do.

educators.heading: A teacher's guide to coding in the classroom
educators.intro: You do not need a computer science background to teach with CodeAlgo Academy. The platform carries the content, so your time goes to the students. These practices help a coding block run smoothly from the first week.

topics.title: Planning with the curriculum
topics.body: Start by deciding what you want students to be able to do by the end of the term, then work backward. Use the curriculum guide to see which concepts come in which order, and where lessons connect to standards such as TEKS, CCSS, and B.E.S.T. Pair coding with a subject you already teach, such as math, so it supports your plans instead of competing with them.

topics.title: Managing the classroom
topics.body: Set up your class before the first session and add students with Clever, Google Classroom, or manual entry. Print login cards with QR codes for younger students so sign-in does not eat up the lesson. Agree on simple routines: where devices live, what to do when stuck, and how to ask for help. Many teachers use an "ask three classmates before me" rule.

topics.title: Using assessment tools
topics.body: Check progress data during the lesson as well as after it. A quick look shows who is racing ahead and who has been on the same level for too long. Use that to decide who needs a short conversation today. Ask students to explain their solution out loud, because a student who can describe the logic has understood it.

topics.title: Making lesson plans work
topics.body: A reliable coding lesson has three parts. Open with a five-minute warm-up that introduces the idea of the day away from the screen. Give students most of the time to work through levels at their own pace, since adaptive learning paths keep each one at the right difficulty. Close by asking two or three students to share what they solved and what was hard.

topics.title: Sharing progress reports
topics.body: Progress reports are most useful when they lead to action. Review them every week or two to spot students who need support and students who are ready for a harder challenge. Bring them to parent conferences and to conversations with school leaders, so families and administrators can see growth over time and not just a final grade.

topics.title: Supporting every learner
topics.body: A coding class always has a wide range of experience, from students who have never typed a line to students who code at home. Let students move at their own pace instead of keeping everyone on the same level. Pair a confident student with one who is unsure, and switch who controls the keyboard so both stay involved. For students who finish early, ask them to solve the same level a different way or to explain their solution to a classmate. For students who struggle, shorten the goal for the day and celebrate each level they complete.

topics.title: Scheduling coding time
topics.body: Consistency matters more than length. Two or three sessions of twenty to thirty minutes a week usually produce steadier progress than one long block. Put coding on the timetable as a fixed slot, and keep a backup plan for days when devices or the network fail. CodeAlgo runs in the browser on the Chromebooks and computers your school already has.

pricing.heading: How to choose the right plan
pricing.intro: The right plan depends on who is learning and for how long. Here is how to think it through before you subscribe.

topics.title: Monthly or annual?
topics.body: Both family plans give your child the same game, lessons, and parent tools. A monthly plan is the flexible choice if you want to see how your child takes to coding before you commit. An annual plan costs less over twelve months and suits families who already know coding will be part of the weekly routine. Learning to code is a gradual skill, so most children get more from steady practice over many months than from a short burst.

topics.title: Planning for more than one child
topics.body: Each child learns on their own profile, with their own progress, levels, and achievements, so siblings of different ages can work at different speeds. You manage every child from one parent account, which means one login for you and one place to see how each of them is doing.

topics.title: What to expect after you subscribe
topics.body: Pick a plan above and log in to your parent account to complete payment. Then add your child's profile and they can start playing. Your first week is a good time to sit with them for a session, set a regular schedule, and agree on screen time. After that, a weekly look at your parent dashboard is enough to stay in touch with their progress.

topics.title: Choosing as a school or district
topics.body: Schools usually start with a simple question: how many students and how many classrooms? Have those numbers ready when you request a quote, along with the grade levels involved and whether you use Clever or Google Classroom for rostering. Districts buying for several schools should use the bulk purchase form so that pricing reflects the full number of schools.

topics.title: Questions to ask before you decide
topics.body: A few questions make the choice easier. How many children will be learning, and how old are they? How many days a week can they realistically practice? Do you want to try coding for a short time first, or are you planning for the whole school year? If you are a teacher or school leader, who else needs to approve the purchase, and when does your budget year start? Having these answers ready will help you choose a plan with confidence, and will help our team give you an accurate quote.

topics.title: Getting the most from your plan
topics.body: Whichever plan you choose, results come from regular use. Two or three short sessions a week, a parent or teacher who checks progress, and a little encouragement when a level feels hard will do more for a child than any feature. If you are unsure which plan fits your situation, send us a message and we will help you decide.

devForum.heading: Getting the most from a workshop
devForum.intro: A workshop works best when it is planned around your school's goals. A little preparation before the session, and a clear plan for afterward, help the training carry over into everyday teaching.

topics.title: Before the session
topics.body: Decide what you want teachers to be able to do when they leave. Share your grade levels, the devices you use, and how students are rostered, so the session can be matched to your setup. Ask teachers to bring a laptop and, if they already have classes, their real class lists. Working with their own students' accounts makes the practice far more useful than a demo.

topics.title: During the session
topics.body: Expect hands-on work, not a lecture. Teachers get the most out of time spent setting up a class, assigning a lesson, and reading a progress report themselves. It also helps to play a few levels as a student, because seeing what learners see makes it easier to help them later. Encourage questions about your own classrooms as they come up.

topics.title: After the session
topics.body: Plan a first coding lesson within a week, while the training is fresh. Choose one or two teachers to act as the go-to people for colleagues, and set a short check-in a few weeks later to share what is working. Schools that schedule a refresher once a term tend to keep their momentum, especially when new staff join.

topics.title: Who should attend
topics.body: Workshops are most effective when the people who will use the platform learn together. Invite the classroom teachers who will run the lessons, and include a school leader or coordinator so that decisions about scheduling and devices can be made in the room. If your school has technology staff who manage rostering or Chromebooks, bring them too. A shared session means everyone hears the same guidance, and teachers leave knowing who to ask when a question comes up later.

topics.title: Questions worth asking
topics.body: Come with real situations from your classrooms. How should we group students with different levels of experience? What does a good first month look like? How do we share progress with families? The more specific the question, the more useful the answer will be for your team.

topics.title: Choosing the right session
topics.body: Teams new to the platform should start with the introduction. Teachers who have used CodeAlgo for a while will get more from the best practices session, and the quick start suits a team with limited time. If your staff has mixed experience, tell us, and we can suggest how to split the group.

internships.heading: How to stand out when you apply
internships.intro: Companies do not expect students to know everything. They look for people who can think clearly, keep learning, and work well with others. These habits will help you show that.

topics.title: Keep a record of what you build
topics.body: Every time you finish a project or solve a hard problem, write down what it was, what you tried, and what finally worked. A short list of real examples is the start of a portfolio. When someone asks what you can do, you will have specific stories to tell instead of a general answer.

topics.title: Practice explaining your code
topics.body: Being able to explain your thinking matters as much as getting the right answer. Pick a problem you solved and describe it out loud to a parent, teacher, or friend: what the goal was, how you broke it into steps, and where you got stuck. If they can follow you, an interviewer will too.

topics.title: Get comfortable with being stuck
topics.body: Professional programmers spend much of their day fixing things that do not work yet. When your code fails, read the error, change one thing at a time, and test again. Learning to stay calm and work through a problem step by step is one of the most valuable skills you can bring to a team.

topics.title: Build good work habits now
topics.body: Show up on time, finish what you start, and ask for help when you need it. Practice writing clear, polite messages, since much of the work in tech happens in writing. Working on a level with a classmate is good practice for the teamwork every internship involves.

topics.title: Prepare a simple resume
topics.body: One page is enough. List your school, the programming languages you have used, the hours of coding you have completed, and two or three projects you are proud of. Ask a teacher or parent to read it and check for mistakes before you send it.

topics.title: Keep learning while you wait
topics.body: Do not stop practicing after you apply. Keep solving problems and adding to your record of projects, so you are ready to talk about your most recent work when a company gets in touch.

topics.title: Ask good questions
topics.body: An interview goes both ways. Come with a few questions about what interns work on, who they learn from, and what a normal day looks like. Curiosity shows that you care about the work and not only about the title.

learnMore.heading: How to start learning to code
learnMore.intro: Anyone can learn to code, and you do not need to be a math genius or own an expensive computer. What you need is a good starting point and regular practice. Here is a path that works for most beginners.

topics.title: Start with block coding
topics.body: Block coding lets you build programs by snapping together colored blocks instead of typing. You learn the big ideas, such as sequences, loops, and conditions, without worrying about spelling or punctuation. It is the easiest way to see how a computer follows instructions, and it is where many young coders begin.

topics.title: Move on to a real language
topics.body: Once the ideas feel familiar, try a text language. Python is a popular first choice because its code reads almost like English. The logic you learned with blocks stays the same. Only the way you write it changes, so the step up is smaller than it looks.

topics.title: Practice a little, often
topics.body: Coding is a skill, like playing an instrument or a sport. Twenty minutes a few times a week beats one long session a month. Each time you practice, your brain gets faster at spotting patterns and remembering how things fit together.

topics.title: Learn to love fixing mistakes
topics.body: Every coder makes mistakes, including the experts. A mistake in code is called a bug, and finding and fixing it is called debugging. When something does not work, read the message, change one thing, and try again. Each bug you fix teaches you something you will not forget.

topics.title: Build things you care about
topics.body: You learn fastest when you are making something you actually want. It could be a simple game, a quiz for your friends, or a drawing made with code. Start small, finish it, and then make it a little better. Finished small projects teach more than big ones you never complete.

topics.title: Use math and logic as you go
topics.body: Coding and math help each other. Counting, patterns, coordinates, and working things out step by step all show up in code. Many students find that math makes more sense after they have used it to make a character move or a score go up.

topics.title: What you need to begin
topics.body: You can start with very little. A computer, Chromebook, or tablet with a web browser is enough, and you do not have to install anything complicated. Set aside a regular time, find a quiet place to focus, and keep a notebook nearby for ideas and for things you want to remember. The most important thing to bring is curiosity. If you like solving puzzles, building things, or asking how something works, you already think like a coder.

topics.title: Learn with other people
topics.body: Share what you build with family, classmates, or a teacher. Explaining your code to someone else helps you understand it better, and seeing how others solved the same problem gives you new ideas. Most software in the world is built by teams, so learning together is good practice for the real thing.

caseStudies.heading: Why coding practice supports math growth
caseStudies.intro: Coding and math draw on the same habits of mind. This is why time spent solving coding problems can show up as growth in the math classroom, and why we look at math results alongside coding activity.

topics.title: Problems are broken into steps
topics.body: To write a program, a student has to split a task into small steps and put them in the right order. That is the same skill needed for a multi-step word problem or a long calculation. Practicing it in a game, where each step gives instant feedback, makes the habit easier to carry into math.

topics.title: Math is used, not just studied
topics.body: In a coding challenge, numbers have a job to do. Students count moves, work with coordinates and angles, use variables, and repeat patterns with loops. Using a concept to reach a goal gives it meaning, and students are more likely to remember an idea they have put to work.

topics.title: Mistakes become part of learning
topics.body: Code rarely works the first time. Students learn to test an idea, see what went wrong, and try again without giving up. That persistence matters in math, where many students stop at the first wrong answer. Coding gives them a safe place to practice being wrong and recovering from it.

topics.title: Each student works at the right level
topics.body: When challenges match a student's grade level and adjust as they improve, students who are behind can catch up without being left out, and students who are ahead stay challenged. Steady work at the right level of difficulty is what produces growth over a semester.

topics.title: Confidence opens the next door
topics.body: A student who has solved hundreds of problems starts to see themselves as someone who can do hard things. That confidence affects which courses they choose, whether they stay with math, and whether a career in technology feels possible. Skills matter, and so does believing those skills are within reach.

topics.title: What helps schools see growth
topics.body: The schools that see the most progress tend to share a few practices. They give coding a regular place in the week instead of treating it as an occasional reward. Teachers look at progress data and step in early when a student stalls. Leaders stay involved and make sure devices and time are protected. Families hear about what their children are building. None of this is complicated, but it has to be consistent, and consistent practice is what turns a promising tool into measurable results.

topics.title: Reading the results on this page
topics.body: The figures above come from platform records and from assessment reports shared by partner schools, and each one names its source. Growth data reflects the schools and time periods shown. Results in any school depend on how often students practice and how the program is used in class, so we share these numbers as evidence of what consistent use can do.
